content.intro: Learn savepoints and partial rollbacks through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Savepoints and Partial Rollbacks matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The main question in savepoints and partial rollbacks is what must stay correct when several statements, errors, or concurrent sessions are involved. Define the transaction boundary and the invariant that must still hold before committing.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Creating a savepoint, Rolling back to a savepoint, Releasing savepoints, Nested transaction misconceptions. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Creating a savepoint
items.text: Creating a savepoint is about keeping multi-step work correct when errors or other sessions intervene. Keep transactions short, define what must succeed together, handle conflicts explicitly, and test using separate sessions in a disposable database.

items.text: Recovery inside multi-step operations begins with a definition of the metric and its grain. Name the numerator, denominator, time zone, null policy, and tie-handling rule before translating the definition into SQL.

content_blocks.expected_output: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes work after the savepoint while keeping the outer transaction open; the final ROLLBACK leaves no changes.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
